extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor/psychoanalysis and educated general readers interested in the theory of wit
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the technical devices and thought-process deviations that produce wit (puns, displacement, nonsense, sophistic errors, automatic replies), illustrated with examples and reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun (sound-based resemblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A wit form in which two words for both meanings resemble each other through slight similarity in structure, rhythmic consonance, a community of vowels, or other similar sound-based resemblance; often accomplished by modifying one vowel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Latin censores liberorum → censores librorum; vowel-modification examples. Anti-pattern: when both words are identical (Heine's 'Calcutta' roast example), the pun is poor because it merely repeats identity rather than exploiting resemblance. Notes: puns operate primarily on sound and are limited as a source of new technique; individuals may reply constantly with puns when in high spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: 'pun' vs 'play on words' (K. Fischer)
rubrics_metrics.description: K. Fischer's technical distinction: 'A pun is a bad play on words, for it does not play with the word as a word, but merely as a sound.' The 'play on words' transfers itself from the sound of the word into the word itself (i.e., meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: evaluate whether the wit operates on sound alone (pun) or on semantic/lexical transfer (play on words). Note the author questions strict separation but preserves the analytical usefulness of the distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning / manifold application of same material
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit that exploits a word or phrase with multiple interpretations (e.g., 'take a bath' read idiomatically vs literally; 'living' meaning alive vs earning a living).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgroup f examples: same word used in 'full' and 'empty' senses. Test: substitute equivalent wording (e.g., 'bathed' for 'take a bath')—if wit disappears, the double-meaning was essential. Double meaning can enable displacement but is analytically separable (double meaning supplies the lexical pivot; displacement supplies the mental tangent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement (psychic-accent shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique whereby the stream of thought is diverted by shifting the psychic accent from the original theme to another, producing a deviation that yields wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: may be independent of specific wording (salmon with mayonnaise) or depend on expression (bath question). Often combines with double meaning (bath, Golden Calf). Analytical tool: reduction/dilation—if changing the mental trend (not merely words) removes wit, displacement was essential. Examples: Heine's 'older than that' retort; bath joke; salmon answer; horse-dealer/Monticello. Reduction method: remove displacement to see whether the joke survives (if not, displacement was essential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on wording versus mental trend
rubrics_metrics.description: Some witticisms hinge on specific verbal formulation (wording-dependent), while others rest on the mental trend or conceptual displacement regardless of particular words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: wording-dependent — bath joke ('have you taken a bath?' vs 'bathed') where alteration destroys the wit; wording-independent — 'salmon with mayonnaise' where the displacement of thought (answer's misdirection) is the core. Use reductions by substituting wording or altering mental emphasis to test dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction method (analytic test for essential elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of analysis in which the joke is 'reduced' or 'dilated' (remove elements or rephrase) to determine which components are essential to the wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: remove or alter suspected elements (wording, double meaning, displacement) and observe whether the witticism survives. If the wit disappears after reduction, the removed element was essential. Frequently used throughout the chapter to distinguish displacement, double meaning, nonsense, and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense as a technical means
rubrics_metrics.description: Advancing something apparently absurd or nonsensical which, however, discloses a sense that transforms nonsense into wit; nonsense can expose other nonsense or create confusion/astonishment purposefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Buy a cannon and make yourself independent' (Ike); modern appendix to 'Never to be born would be best for mortal man' (Fliegende Blätter); screen-between-beds anecdote. Function: nonsense-wit often imitates stupidity to reflect or expose another stupidity, or it attaches a nonsensical appendix to reveal hollowness of a prior statement. Reduction will replace the nonsense with explicit sense, eliminating the wit (becomes plain cynicism or statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistic faulty thinking (semblance of logic / fallacious reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit that employs fallacious, sophistic, or faulty lines of reasoning—using a façade of logic to conceal errors such as illegitimate connections, misapplied 'and/or', or treating possibilities as actualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cake/liqueur exchange (illegitimate linkage 'for it'); marriage-agent evasions (treating separate defects individually rather than summing them); borrowed kettle defense (three mutually exclusive claims presented as compatible); equating possibility with actuality (Rabbi example). Evaluation: identify the hidden logical error the joke exploits; the humor often lies in the evident but fallacious 'logic' of the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic errors of thought (echo / automatic confirmation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit produced by automatic, stereotyped, or reflexive responses—repetition or echoing that amplifies or endorses assertions without genuine evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: marriage-agent with assistant echoing phrases ('Like a pine tree' → 'Like a pine tree'); assistant acting as automatic confirmer of claims. Mechanism: the automatic repetition functions as rhetorical support and becomes comic by highlighting emptiness or absurdity. Look for echoes, automatic affirmations, and rehearsed confirmations as technical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization-wit (show-side of façade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witticisms that serve to portray or caricature a character trait (e.g., a mendacious, impudent marriage agent), where the 'wit' functions as an illustration of personality rather than only a logical/linguistic device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: the author treats characterization as the 'show-side' of the joke's façade and often defers reduction; such jokes may combine characterization with other devices (double meaning, displacement). Evaluation should distinguish the expressive/performative role (characterization) from the technical mechanism producing the laugh.
